job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Pedro. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm in the power lab at Ridgemoor College, bench-testing inverters for my master's in renewable energy systems. Afternoons I tutor maths to teenagers at 15 an hour, which covers about a third of my rent in the student flat. In the evening I apply for jobs, usually two or three, and then I cook for the flat because I'm the only one who can make a decent lentil stew. It's a full day, but nothing in it pays enough.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical engineering, a pass. My final project was a solar charge controller for a primary school, and it worked, but my marks were dragged down by a bad maths exam in the second year. I had no internship; I was tutoring instead. My dad was a postal worker and has a small pension, so there's no family money, and I owe about twenty-eight thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief and a letdown at the same time. Relief because a robot isn't taking my place on day one. Letdown because I keep hearing it will change everything and then the grid still runs on spreadsheets from 2009. I'd tell my flatmates the hype is mostly marketing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my situation is simply my situation. Debt of twenty-eight thousand, a pass degree and no internship, in a town with maybe four employers for electrical graduates. That isn't AI's fault, it's the economy. I'd be anxious even with no AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep tutoring, finish the master's with a better mark than my bachelor's, and apply to the grid operator and the big installers every week. I'd also email three smaller solar firms directly, because they don't advertise. I use an AI tool now and then to debug my code, and I'd carry on with that, but it saves me maybe ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, a bit tense. There's no fear of the future exactly, just money anxiety that sits behind everything, like a hum from a transformer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned four employers nearby. What happens if none of them hires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I move, probably to the city two hours away and rent a room with strangers. That costs a deposit I don't have. My plan would be to borrow it from my aunt, which I really don't want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tutoring hours would go up, not down, so what I'd cut is my sleep. After that, the train fare home for my dad's birthday. I'd hate that one.

say: I'd tell my flatmates AI is mostly **marketing** and the grid still runs on old spreadsheets.
I'd say what we really need is public investment in energy jobs.
think: My problem is **debt**, a pass degree and no internship, not AI.
Only about four local employers hire electrical graduates, so I'd be anxious with or without AI.
do: Keep **tutoring** and aim for a better master's mark than my bachelor's.
Email three small **solar firms** directly, since they don't advertise.
Keep using an AI tool now and then to debug code.
feel: A bit flat and **tense**: money worry hums behind everything.
S0.quote: There's no fear of the future exactly, just money anxiety that sits behind everything, like a hum from a transformer.
fieldNote: He separates AI worry from **money** worry and says the second is the real one.
Steady with tools: uses AI occasionally and says it saves about ten minutes.
Jokes to cope, but the debt figure comes up unprompted.

steps.text: Keep tutoring maths teenagers at 15 an hour
Email three small solar firms directly each month
Finish the master's with a better mark than the bachelor's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and it's going to hit the people at the start of careers first. If software writes the draft reports and checks the drawings, there's less for a graduate to do on day one. I'd say that out loud and ask that firms and the government keep funding graduate schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my kind of job survives but there will be fewer places on it. Grid work still needs someone to climb a pole, but the planning and the paperwork around it get done by software. So four vacancies become two, and I'm applying against people with better marks. I think it's probably me who loses that fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into the parts of the work that software won't take quickly: commissioning, site testing and safety checks. I'd get my low-voltage safety ticket, which costs about 300, and look at installer firms rather than design offices. I'd also learn to use the AI tools properly rather than now and then, because a graduate who uses them well can do the paperwork of two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit irritated. I don't mind the technology; I mind that the firms get the savings and the graduates get the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools properly. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, one evening a week, working through the tools my master's tutor already uses for load forecasting. I'd rather build something small, like a script that sorts a site's meter readings, and put it on my CV. If the machine is going to do my first job, I'd rather be the person running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the 300 for the safety ticket come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eleven weeks of tutoring on top of what I do now. My housemate Tomasz says I'm mad, but a ticket makes me cheaper and safer to hire for a small installer. If I don't get the ticket I'm just a degree with no hands.

say: I'd say it hits **new graduates** first, and firms and government should keep funding graduate schemes.
I'd stay loud about it online.
think: My kind of job survives, but **fewer places** on it: four vacancies become two.
I'd be competing with people who have better marks, and I'd probably lose.
do: Get a low-voltage **safety ticket** for about 300 from extra tutoring.
Target **installer firms** rather than design offices.
Spend an evening a week using AI tools properly and build a small **meter-reading script**.
feel: **Uneasy** and irritated that firms keep the savings while graduates carry the risk.
S1.quote: If the machine is going to do my first job, I'd rather be the person running it.
fieldNote: Sees his edge in **site work**, commissioning and safety, not desk work.
Steady adaptability shows: he commits to learning the tools but wants a small, concrete project first.
Blame lands on firms and the lack of a public graduate scheme.

steps.text: Pay about 300 for a low-voltage safety ticket from extra tutoring
Build a small script that sorts site meter readings for my CV
Apply to installer firms rather than design offices
Add eleven weeks of tutoring to cover the ticket fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough and I'd say it loudly, at the college, online, to my MP. Governments don't plan on that timescale. If it's true, we need a basic income or a big public jobs programme and we need it before 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. I finish the master's in about a year, which means I'd graduate into the exact moment when software can do the entry-level thinking work. My debt doesn't shrink because AGI shows up. I'd have no savings, no internship and a degree whose entry jobs are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase the hands-on side: grid maintenance, solar installation, anything that needs a person on site, because the robots for that don't arrive until around 2031. I'd take any paid site work, even for a small firm, and stop the master's if I could get a decent job. I'd also lobby the college and my MP, and join a graduate campaign group if there is one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hollow. I'd be scared, but I'd also feel strangely focused. There'd be no time to be fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd phone him and say I'm fine, which he'd know isn't true. Then he'd tell me about the strike at the sorting office in 1989 and how people stuck together. I'd want to hear that story, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there's no site work to be had?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd need the government to step in, and I'd go and march for it. I'd rather do anything than sit in a student flat waiting for the debt to arrive.

say: I'd say two years is **not enough** and demand a basic income or public jobs programme.
I'd say it to my MP and to everyone at the college.
think: I'd graduate into the moment software can do **entry-level thinking work**, with debt unchanged.
I'd have no savings, no internship and a degree whose entry jobs are gone.
do: Chase **site work** such as grid maintenance and solar installation before robots arrive around 2031.
Take any paid site job, even small, and **stop the master's** if I could.
Join a **graduate campaign** group and lobby my MP.
S2.quote: My debt doesn't shrink because AGI shows up. I'd have no savings, no internship and a degree whose entry jobs are gone.
fieldNote: Quick to move toward **hands-on** work and the 2031 robot gap, a pragmatic read of the card.
Willing to drop the master's for a paid job, which shows how thin his cushion is.
Turns to politics and collective action rather than blaming himself.

steps.text: Apply for grid maintenance and solar installer jobs that need people on site
Write to my MP about a public jobs programme for graduates
Join a graduate campaign group and go to its first march
Ask the college hardship fund for help with the next rent payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like a longer fuse. I'd say we should use it to build something, like retraining funds, a graduate guarantee and a public stake in the AI companies. I'd say it in the union branch of my tutoring agency, if they have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but not paralysed. If I land a site-based first job by next year, I'd have about four years of useful experience before 2031. After that, who knows. The scary version is that I get no first job and the experience gap never closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and then take any decent first job in grid or solar work, even for less than I'd like. I'd save 150 a month toward the debt, because wiping it matters more than a nice flat. I'd keep learning the AI tools and aim at a role where I supervise software and check its output, since the checking side is where an engineer still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panic, more grind. Having time to plan is a small luxury, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a public stake in the companies. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean that if software does the work, some of the money it makes should go to the public, through a tax or a share. That would pay for retraining and basic support. I don't think the companies will volunteer it, so voters have to ask. It's not a socialist idea, it's just a fair split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the 150 a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From a first salary that doesn't exist yet. If it's a typical graduate salary I could do it by cutting my phone plan and cooking more. If I'm still on tutoring, then it's closer to 50.

say: I'd say we should use five years to build a **graduate guarantee** and retraining funds.
I'd argue the public should share in the money AI makes.
think: With a site-based first job soon I'd get about **four years** of experience before robots arrive.
The scary version is no first job and an **experience gap** that never closes.

Save **150 a month** toward the debt.

steps.text: Take a first job in grid or solar work even if the pay is low
Save 150 a month toward the 28,000 debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time to retrain, and I'd say that out loud. I'd say schools and colleges should add AI skills for every engineering student, and that employers should keep paying for trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly steady. I'd be 34 by 2036, with ten years of experience if I get a job soon, probably clear of the debt, and I'd have a real chance to move into a role that supervises systems. The worry would be if I don't land the first job within a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the first grid or solar job I could get, and spend about five hours a week on a skill that sits close to the machines, like control systems or battery storage. I'd save for a deposit on a small flat. And I'd stay in touch with the college, because their alumni network is where my first interview will come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. Not calm, but there's room to breathe. I could even picture a Sunday where I don't open the job portal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger student in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't skip the internship, even if it's unpaid, because I did and I regret it. And learn the tools, but also learn something that needs your hands or your judgement. I wish somebody had told me that in first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not calm. What's the remaining worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That ten years sounds long but my first two are the ones that decide everything. If those years go badly, I'd be 26 with nothing built. So I'd still push hard right now.

say: I'd say colleges should teach **AI skills** to every engineering student.
I'd say employers should keep paying for trainees.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 with a decent career and maybe **no debt**, if I land a first job soon.
The worry is that my **first two years** decide everything.
do: Take the first grid or solar job and learn **battery storage** or control systems.
Spend five hours a week on that skill and save for a flat **deposit**.

S4.quote: Don't skip the internship, even if it's unpaid, because I did and I regret it.

steps.text: Take the first grid or solar job offered after the master's

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one scares me most, because the debt and the timing collide and there'd be no time to adjust. What would help is a graduate guarantee, paid trainee places with the grid operator, and some debt relief if entry jobs vanish. I'd also like a clear, honest government plan about what happens to my generation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't asking for a free ride. We're asking for a first rung. If I get it I'll climb, but I can't climb from the pavement.

headlineQuote: We're asking for a first rung. If I get it I'll climb, but I can't climb from the pavement.
portrait: Pedro is 24, doing a master's in **renewable energy**, living in a student flat and tutoring maths for cash.
He has a pass in electrical engineering, **no internship** and about twenty-eight thousand in debt.
His dad's small postal pension means no family money, and his view of the world is **progressive**, favouring public investment.
He uses AI tools now and then, and when pushed he commits to learning them and heading for **site work**.
His mood runs from anxious to **alarmed**, driven more by debt and timing than by the technology itself.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture scares him most, because debt and timing collide with no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A **graduate guarantee**: paid trainee places with the grid operator and some debt relief.
An honest **government plan** for his generation.
